analysis.one_liner: Tightens oversight of for-profit colleges and expands loan relief for defrauded students.
analysis.headline: The PROTECT Students Act, with 27 Senate cosponsors, was referred to the Senate education committee in March 2019 and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets for-profit colleges, which receive billions in federal student aid and GI Bill money each year. It would restore the old 85/15 rule requiring for-profit schools to get at least 15% of revenue from non-federal sources, count veterans' benefits in that calculation, and create a review process for schools converting to nonprofit status. It would also require career programs to leave graduates earning enough to repay their loans, ban forced arbitration of student claims, create an enforcement unit and a central complaint system at the Education Department, and make it easier for misled borrowers to get their loans discharged.
analysis.who_benefits: Students and borrowers, especially veterans and low-income students recruited by for-profit colleges, gain stronger protection against misleading recruiting, high debt with poor job prospects, and forced arbitration. Taxpayers also gain because federal aid would flow only to programs whose graduates can actually repay their loans.

how_it_helps.text: Restores the 85/15 rule for for-profit colleges and counts GI Bill and Defense Department education funds as federal revenue, closing the loophole that let schools run almost entirely on federal money.
Requires career education programs to meet debt-to-earnings standards, with warnings to enrolled students and loss of federal aid eligibility for failing programs.

Lets borrowers seek loan discharge when a school misled them or engaged in misconduct, and allows state attorneys general and nonprofit legal groups to file group claims on borrowers' behalf, with automatic discharge if the Department fails to decide within 18 months.

Bans colleges from using forced arbitration or other limits that block students from suing in court, and creates an enforcement unit plus a centralized, anonymous complaint system for suspicious practices by schools and loan servicers.
Establishes a cross-agency oversight committee (Education, Justice, SEC, FTC, VA, Defense, CFPB and others) and requires an annual 'For-Profit College Warning List' for parents and students.

analysis.who_pays: For-profit college companies and their investors, whose federal aid revenue could fall if programs fail the 85/15 test or debt-to-earnings standards; online program managers and lead-generation companies that sell recruiting services to colleges; loan servicers facing new complaint tracking and oversight. Federal loan discharges for defrauded borrowers are paid for by taxpayers.
analysis.who_pays_short: For-profit college companies and loan servicers

drawbacks.text: Cutting off federal aid to failing programs, while protecting students from bad debt, could also close some schools mid-enrollment or reduce access to career training in areas where for-profit schools are the main option, forcing students to transfer or re-enroll elsewhere.
Loan discharges under the borrower defense provision are paid with federal funds, so the cost of schools' misconduct falls partly on taxpayers rather than only on the schools.
The bill imposes new compliance and reporting burdens on any institution offering career education programs, including nonprofit and public colleges, not just for-profit chains.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real but small: students who enroll in programs that leave them unable to repay loans currently bear the cost of bad training, and shifting that cost back to the schools that made the promises is the bill's central purpose. The main risks are legitimate — aid cutoffs can strand enrolled students, and discharges cost taxpayers — but the bill includes warning periods, appeal processes, and transition rules designed to soften them.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee in March 2019; the committee never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Maggie Hassan introduced the bill on March 26, 2019, joined by Sens. Durbin and Brown, and it was read twice and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day.
Twenty-seven senators — 26 Democrats and 1 Independent — cosponsored the bill.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the initial referral; the bill never advanced again before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit college companies kept receiving federal student aid and GI Bill dollars under the existing rules, with no new enforcement unit, no restored 85/15 rule, and no expanded borrower discharges. Borrowers defrauded by predatory schools got no new relief.

against.name: For-profit college industry
against.role: Sector facing new revenue limits and enforcement
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal oversight measures like gainful employment rules and the 85/15 revenue test through lobbying campaigns during this period.

sides.party_line_note: All 27 cosponsors were Democrats plus one Independent; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-chaired committee never moved the bill.

industries.note: The bill's main target: it could lose federal aid eligibility if federal money (including GI Bill funds) exceeds 85% of revenue or if graduates' earnings don't support their debt, and it faces a new cross-agency enforcement committee and public warning list. These schools' revenue comes largely from federal student aid paid by ordinary students, so their interest in keeping the current rules runs against the students the bill protects.

industries.industry: Online program managers and lead generators
industries.note: Companies that sell recruiting, lead generation, and program administration to colleges are defined in the bill and brought under federal oversight as third-party contractors, including revenue-sharing arrangements between schools and contractors.
Servicers would fall under a centralized complaint tracking system with mandatory response deadlines and public reporting of complaint volumes per servicer.

industries.industry: Nonprofit and public colleges with career certificate programs
industries.note: Gainful employment debt-to-earnings standards apply to career programs at all types of institutions, adding compliance work for nonprofit and public schools, though the enforcement and warning-list provisions concentrate on for-profits.
